utterances.text: I'm going to be going specifically to page 3 in the English and pages 2 continuing onto page 3 of the B/C/S. Mr. Theunens, coming up before you is a transcript from an audio recording between General Mladic and Lieutenant-Colonel Milisav. This recording was recovered as part of the 2010 Serbian MUP search of premises associated to Mr. Mladic's family. Did you review this transcript which relates to events in Sibenik and Zadar during proofing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, any time-frame for the conversation? Oh, you wanted to ask the witness about that. Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. We reviewed the transcript during the proofing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Based on your analysis of events, can you tell the approximate time-period --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Judge, I'm just pausing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Mr. Mladic should pause, not you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Again, based on your analysis of events, can you tell us the approximate time-period in which this conversation occurred?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would say this is the August/September 1991 time-period.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: At the top of the page, we see General Mladic states: "In Zadar, they're blocked. They are asking for negotiations at 1000 hours. We'll stop firing to see if they will permit a normal evacuation and that everything is all right." General Mladic shortly thereafter states: "If they do not agree, then we will embark on the destruction of Zadar, and then they will probably see what has hit Zadar and will permit you a peaceful evacuation, like Sinj." Do you have any comments on the -- this part of the conversation, based on the materials that you've reviewed?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the conversation refers to the situations in Northern Dalmatia at that time; i.e., the Croats have blocked a number of JNA barracks and garrisons. And in this specific conversation, General Mladic is explaining how he intends to act, depending of the Croatian response to a request to evacuate these JNA facilities, i.e., to remove the pop -- the -- the people, the personnel, and the equipment from these facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have page 8 of the English and page 6 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, I'd like to go part by part through these statements by General Mladic. First, starting with the quote of General Mladic where he states: "Nothing will get out of Dalmatia except children under the age of 10, if they carry on like this." Do you have any comments on this initial statement?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would say it -- it reflects General Mladic's mindset and -- and -- I would -- in relation to or in response to the Croatian blockade of JNA barracks and garrisons in that area, and with "they" he refers to Croatian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This exchange continues Lieutenant-Colonel Milisav stating: "That's what I said. If we get hurt here, then they from 301 to 306, and these ones here, they will have to pay." General Mladic then states: "Listen, Milisav, not from 301 to 306. All that is older than 10 and younger than 75 will come to harm in Sibenik, and we will not leave a single house standing, unless they finish the job like it was done in Sinj." Lieutenant-Colonel Milisav then states: "All right."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If may just interject, please. Mr. Theunens, do you by any chance know what 301 and 306 mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I haven't been able to check a map of the area, but usually these figures are used for geographic features. But that is, I would say, an educated guess at this stage because I didn't have an opportunity to look at the map and to see whether there was a feature 301 and a feature 306 which again, extrapolating, could imply that were Croatian forces on that location. But again, this is just drawn from these five lines of conversation without looking at the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But it looks like Mr. Mladic's response relates to age - I'm not quite sure - and not geography. When he says "not only 301 to 306 but all that is under 10 and over 75." Years.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the reason I referred to a geographic location is, as I mentioned, because I have seen similar figures -- I mean, similar manner of describing geographic features. And then obviously it's not just a feature but it's the forces located that feature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, and I don't know if it would further assist the Chamber or if Mr. Theunens could also further assist us, but if Mr. Theunens is able maybe to identify a map via the Registry, we are willing to go and look if -- for one if you'd-like that done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To provide Mr. Theunens with an unmarked map of the area, would that cause any objections? No. No objections. So if you give it to the Victims and Witness Section so that they can provided to Mr. Theunens. Mr. Theunens, the reference to the job finished in Sinj, does that ring any bell to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand that the -- the -- the JNA garrison in Sinj was -- I mean, again, based on what is written there, allowed to -- to leave under peaceful conditions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What does this part of the conversation show about General Mladic's intentions concerning the uses of force -- forces under his commander?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Objection as to calling for speculation and going beyond the expertise of the witness. I don't believe now he is a psychological expert as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber is able to interpret this part of the conversation without the assistance of the witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Does this conversation at all show how General Mladic exercised his authority, or is there an exercise of authority in this conversation?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours, it's -- as conversation between a superior and a subordinate, and the superior gives instructions to the subordinate.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: On Tuesday, at transcript page 20239, you indicated that there was a pattern between how General Mladic exercised his authority while he was in Croatia and when he was a commander of the VRS. Are these statements by him consistent with this pattern?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are, Your Honours. My impression or my conclusion of -- of the way how General Mladic commanded the VRS while he was commander of the Main Staff is that he is very much focused on the goal he wants to achieve and he wants his subordinates to achieve, and much less concerned of any potential constraints that could inhibit [Realtime transcript read in error "prohibit"] achieving that goal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Based on your review of materials related to the 9th Corps campaign in Croatia, were there any reports that crimes were committed during that campaign?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Again, I would object as to the scope of the same being outwith the indictment. We've had evidence that the campaign, as it is referred to now, started in June of 1991. Surely the indictment does not cover June of 1991. I think we need to have this issue resolved once and for all so the Defence know what is the Prosecution's case that we must address.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber considers the answer to the question or at least the question relevant in view of potential context to be given and parallels and to -- possibly to be drawn. You may answer the question, Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Before doing so, I would just like to make a small correction to the transcript. At the last line of page 51 I mentioned "inhibit" instead of "prohibit." And to answer the question, in Part 1 of the report, pages 171 and following, I discuss documents -- I mean, JNA documents concerning alleged crimes that were committed in Skabrnja and Nadin on 18 and -- and in particular, 19 of November 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you one question, Mr. Theunens. In relation to the conversation which was recorded, you said it shows how he uses his authority. The portions read were very much like, "if," "then," which means that any authority is not exercised yet, although it may show some inclination to do something. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours. I mean, he is not giving a strict military order. There is a lot of "if" and "then." But at the same time, if you put yourself in the position of the subordinate, it gives an impression of -- of -- of how General Mladic sees what should be done. In a sense, it -- I mean, the choice of wording and threats that are implied I would say create quite the impression among the subordinate that they have to be ready to -- to do whatever General Mladic wants them to do and that this can go very far what he wants them to do if certain conditions are not fulfilled. So he's not going to -- apparently he's not going to reconsider the situations if certain things are done or not done by the enemy, but the subordinates have to be ready that if indeed the -- the enemy does certain things or fails to do certain things, then General Mladic's instructions are very clear. And he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But if -- are these instructions already? You say he's not going to reconsider. What makes you believe that he is not going to reconsider. If I say, if this and this happens, I will do that. It happened in my life that I later considered it wiser not to do what I announced to do and no one would have known in advance whether I would reconsider this announcement of action to be taken. Would you agree with that as well, or do you have any specific reason to say that he would not reconsider, even if he didn't announce that he would reconsider. But is it reasonable to assume that everyone who announces certain action, that, automatically, that means that that person would not reconsider it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You know, Your Honour, I understand your -- your comment. But I think we have to be conscious of the context in which these -- in which General Mladic expresses himself. He is not talking on -- as a person. I would say he is talking as a military commander. And communication - and again, we can find that in the doctrine [indiscernible]. But the subordinate expects from the commander instructions and guidelines and the subordinate will act upon what the commander says. If a commander says certain things on one day and then he says the other day the opposite, that has -- gives a negative impression of the commander's authority because the subordinates will say, you know, he is talking again. But this is not a kind of command style General Mladic practiced. My understanding after reviewing all the documents is that if he makes certain -- if he gives certain instructions or -- like here he makes certain threats, that he is very serious about it, and that it's unlikely that he will change his view unless maybe because he is forced by outside circumstances. So I think we should make a distinction between I would call it a more personal conversation between two individuals as opposed to here a conversation between a military commander and a subordinate officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which doesn't change in any way that are no clear instructions here given for the situation which is considered to to potentially develop.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I agree with you, Your Honours. But I think -- again, we don't know how the situation ended -- I mean, we know how the situation ended. I understand the Zadar garrison and the artillery centre were evacuated in a "peaceful manner," that the JNA managed to withdraw its personnel and its equipment there. From the top of my head, I don't know of any garrisons where there was no evacuation, so it is difficult to -- to -- to say whether or not General Mladic would have implemented this threat if there had been no peaceful evacuation by the enemy as he had expressed it from them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll never know. To some extent, it's speculation. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, I'd like to return to a military doctrine on this point that we were just discussing. Can a commander give a conditional order?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, a commander can do anything. But from a doctrinal point of view, an order has to be clear and concise because if you have confusion among the subordinates, then the commander's intent will most likely not be implemented in the manner the commander wanted it to do -- to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'd like to just come to maybe a quicker close to this section. If you could -- I just need to you confirm a couple parts of Part 1 of your report. If you could please go to paragraph 4 on page 169, continuing through to page 170, could you please fully tell us or completely read the conclusions you reached on what the 9th Corps monthly overview reports showed in terms of the crimes recorded in their own corps units and commands.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You want me to read or to summarise?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, I -- you -- you -- it's -- it's pretty clearly stated here, so you're welcome to read it if you would like.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The 9th Corps prepares monthly overview reports of the crimes that have been recorded in the corps' units and commands and the measures that have been taken. These reports show that wilful abandonment and desertion of the armed forces, failing or refusion to go carry out orders are the most common crimes, and that there is a functioning system for military justice to take care of these crimes. "These reports which are signed by the corps commander, do not include serious crimes, including violations of the laws of armed conflict that, at least according to OB reports, have been allegedly committed by members of the SAO Krajina TO and/or other forces while participating in combat operations under the command of the JNA 9th Corps. This situation is the same for the quarterly 'analysis of unusual incidents' covering the first quarter of 1992, Major-General Ratko Mladic submits to the 2nd Military District on the 1st of April, 1992."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In this paragraph are you citing to multiple reports both from General Vukovic or Vuckovic and General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. And I compared those with, for example, reports by security organs concerning events in Skabrnja on 18 and 19 November 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did the reported crimes in the Croatian Krajina become publicly known during the course of 1991 and early 1992?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, they became -- the events in Skabrnja, there was -- as I mentioned in my report, there was a complaint by the Croats to the European Community Monitoring Mission quite soon after these alleged crimes took place, and the ECMM then requested access to the area from the command of the military naval district, which was the superior command of the 9th Corps, and on the other hand there is also a Human Rights Watch report from January 1992 that was sent to General Kadijevic as well as president of Serbia, then Mr. Milosevic. I mean, these are just two examples.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: On page 8 of Part 2, you discuss a 30 April 1992 entry from the published notes of Borislav Jovic, where it was agreed to replace General Vukovic of the 2nd Military District with Ratko Mladic. Among the people present at this meeting were Slobodan Milosevic, Radovan Karadzic, Momcilo Krajisnik, and Nikola Koljevic. Based on the documents you reviewed in this case, would any of these individuals have been aware - I believe you already mentioned President Milosevic - of the reported crimes committed by units under General Mladic's command?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, given the fact that there is an answer by the -- there's a written reply, I'm sorry, by the chef de cabinet of President Milosevic to the Human Rights Watch report, I think it's reasonable to assume that President Milosevic was made aware of the contents of that report which doesn't only address Skabrnja but also other parts of Croatia where the JNA and subordinate units were active.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Prior to April 1992, was there any co-ordination between these individuals at this 30 April 1992 meeting, so co-ordination between individuals from the Bosnian Serb leadership, the SFRY, and the Republic of Serbia, related to the transformation of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, from -- from Borisav Jovic's published memoirs, one can conclude that a number of the aforementioned individuals meet and indeed at different occasions discuss the future of the JNA. I also remember that, for example, Mr. Martic and Mr. Babic were invited in 1991, early 1992, to meetings of what remained of the SFRY Presidency. And also there, the future of the JNA was -- in Croatia was being discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution at this time tenders from the bar table 65 ter 17314 and 65 ter 17315 related to the public dissemination and notification of crimes committed in Croatia. These materials consist of the letter from Helsinki Watch to Slobodan Milosevic and Veljko Kadijevic, which the mention has mentioned, and a list of press coverage related to the same letter which indicates that it was widely covered internationally and within the region.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can we have some clarification. The witness has been talking about Human Rights Watch, which is not the same as Helsinki Watch.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I might have misspoke.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I meant the same document so I can check who it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I take it that if there remains any confusion about that, that the parties will report that, and that we act on the assumption that Helsinki Watch -- the report which was mentioned as be a Human Rights Watch, that that's the same as the Helsinki Watch, and the Chamber of course will seriously consider any further reports on this. Apart from that, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We would again object to the relevance of the same; in particular, the other news coverage which this witness has not discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, therefore it's bar tabled. The witness was asked about public knowledge about these matters and that is apparently what the Prosecution wants to establish, that at least there was -- there were publications about it. Mr. Weber, you said you want to bar table it. That is, two documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour. And I see it's a letter from Helsinki Watch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's Helsinki Watch.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stand corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And it's 65 ter 17314, and then the distribution of this is 65 ter 17315.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, the first document -- single document, Helsinki Watch.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 17314 receives Exhibit P3052.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And document 17315 receives number P3053, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Also admitted into evidence. Mr. Weber you -- yes. May I take it that the first number for 17 -- yes, there we have it, 3052. Mr. Weber, you announced what I understood to be the Helsinki Watch letter and the publications. Now, you also referred to a response or at least the witness referred to a response by the chef de cabinet of Milosevic. Is that part of it or is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll be guided by you. I'm happy to tender as many documents as the Chamber would like relating to these matters, so I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, as many -- I was --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I can tender that document too, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the speakers kindly not overlap for the sake of interpretation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will. Isn't it, Mr. Weber? Yes, the Chamber would like the response to the letter of Helsinki Watch to have it in evidence as well. So if you would please tender it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thanks, Your Honour. I was just marking it as a to do. Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 14429.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The document coming up before you, Mr. Theunens, is a 9th Corps order from Ratko Mladic dated 22 April 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weber. Did you present the response?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll have to -- I'm sorry. If I can look it up during the next break, I'm happy to do it, and I will immediately provide the 65 ter number after the -- the recess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Ms. Stewart's a little faster than I am. It's 65 ter 17316.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps we have it briefly on our screens so that we ... Now, I notice that this apparently is not the original but it's a publication in which apparently the response is reproduced. Do you have a -- an original one or don't you have that, Mr. Weber?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't believe so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then this is better categorised as what was published at the time and perhaps falls into the category of public dissemination of the -- the discussion on the matter. We'll be able to carefully, first of all, to see whether this is a response to what you presented. And I see that the English translation shows a nice B/C/S text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, it's the original -- the original is in English, yes. I'm -- apologise. One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we see the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And -- could we have the English --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The entire --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The entire -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, there it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is very difficult to read it. Let me ... One second, please, Mr. Weber, so we have an opportunity to look at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would give us just one minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections? But more in the category of dissemination of the information.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I haven't seen the text of the article that this is contained in. I would have an issue with that coming in since we don't have the text of that, and I would think that would not be appropriate to come in without having it be translated. But as for this coming in, in the context of the witness's testimony, I do not have an objection to this, the actual response from the Chief of Staff of the president of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, would you then -- you can do two things: Either can you upload the publication in its entirety -- and it has been uploaded, but translate the publication in its entirety which would then include the text of the response; or you can now state that you will only rely on this document for purposes of reading the response.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could please check in to see what we have, and if we could just mark it for identification right now so we can ask for a replacement. And I just want to note for the record that it is cited in Mr. Theunens's report just so that we have it on the record, this version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number under which the document will be marked for identification is?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 17316 receives number P3054, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P3054 is marked for identification. I noticed that that -- but perhaps we could ask the witness who dealt with it. The language used as far as -- especially in the second paragraph, where it reads: "The president of the Republic of Serbia asked the competent organs of the Republic of Serbia to investigate the abuses ..." Could I ask you whether there's any chance that there is some problem in using the English language for what originally is the Republic of Serbia and Republika Srpska, but that could not be yet in February 1992. So I'm a bit -- I'm puzzled by it's not within our competence, more or less, but we -- at the same time, we asked the competent organs to investigate. Yes, yes, for involvement of the citizens of the Republic of Serbia, I see. So the gist is we are not competent because it was not on our territory, but we'll nevertheless investigate to see whether of any of our citizens is involved in those crimes and whether they should be brought to justice. Is that a correct understanding of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could I please have exhibit -- or, I'm sorry, 65 ter 14429.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, this will be another document from your report. This is a 9th Corps order from General Mladic dated 22 April 1992 concerning the provision of arms and equipment for the police units of the RSK. Was this order issued after the Vance Plan was agreed to?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could you please explain to us what General Mladic orders under item 1?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, General Mladic orders to assist the transfer of manpower of the corps, so the JNA 9th Corps, to the RSK MUP. And by assisting, I mean that they should be given, as the text states, personal arms and one combat set of ammunition similar to what military persons are issued with.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: On pages 175 to 179 of Part 1, you discuss the Vance Plan and related events that occurred in the 9th Corps zone of responsibility through the end of April 1992. Could you please tell us whether this order and other actions by General Mladic were in accordance with the Vance Plan?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'll object again. This is beyond the scope of the expertise of this witness for which he has been noticed under Rule 65 ter and Rule 94 bis. Again, we're going into something that at best could be labelled historical expert testimony, but in actuality is Prosecution closing arguments making their assertions of how documents and evidence should be interpreted which is not appropriate for this phase of the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is denied. This could be considered as background information, especially how the accused -- whether the accused in the past has acted in accordance with -- with international political developments or not. At the same time, Mr. Weber, you may have noticed that I had to consult with my colleagues several times. Background and context should not become the foreground, and please keep that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you very much. I understand that. I was just trying to lead this evidence, and I thought this one document kind of makes the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]...

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Just briefly, Your Honour. For background factual evidence to come in, the Prosecution ought to be held to the standard of bringing background factual witnesses. To have an in-house former member of their staff be the only witness about background factual issues for this Chamber to reply upon in this case I believe is not in accord with the jurisprudence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In evaluation of the evidence, of course, the Chamber will not just rely on what the witness says but also the documentary -- on the documents underlying what the witness expressed as his expert opinion. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know what you're saying. If maybe later today I could just have a moment in time to -- to just understand what you just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: But, Mr. Theunens --

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: -- could you -- could you -- I don't remember if you remember my question before the discussion. Go ahead, then.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. And, again, without going in too many details, but one of the provisions of the Vance Plan is to demilitarise the -- the areas called United Nations Protected Areas in Croatia, and this meant that all armed forces had to be withdrawn, JNA, ZNG, TO, anything else, or demilitarised and demobilised; I mean, those a remaining in the territory of the UNPAs except for lightly armed police force, and I have explained that on page 176 of Part 1 of my report. What we see in this order by General Mladic is that he undertakes active steps to circumvent the demilitarisation part by handing over personnel and/or weapons that were military to this local Serb police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: At this time, the Prosecution tenders 65 ter 14429 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We would object for the reasons previously stated on the record, that this relates to events that are outside the subject matter and geographic scope of the indictment that was given to the Defence as notice of the charges to defend against in this trial. To at the eleventh hour receive an expansion of the substance and the geographic scope of the indictment, impinges upon the ability of the Defence to address the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is basically on the same basis as the previous ones and is denied. I think we still needed the number for the document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, document 14429 receives number P3055.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I would now like to turn to a discussion of the Bosnian Serb six strategic goals. On page 36 of Part 2, you state that these strategic goals are an order of priority with the first being the separation of the Serbian people from the other two national communities. What is the reason you -- you conclude that this first strategic goal takes priority over the other five?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think you mentioned in order of priority. My conclusion is based on the fact how Mr. Karadzic presents the strategic goals at the 12th Assembly Session and also to a lesser extent then how this goal actually continues to be covered in the military documents, not only the directive for further operations but also subsequent orders and subordinate orders to implement these corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: On page 41 of Part 2, you conclude: "The six strategic goals are the basis for the plans to seize and control territory, establish a Serb republic, defend defined borders, and separate the ethnic groups in BiH." I would like to have you further explain each part of this opinion. First, could you tell us, how were the strategic goals a plan to seize and control territory?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean, by looking at the contents -- by looking at the actual goals, and I will just -- I will read the second one, because I think it's the most obvious, if you need -- if you want to establish a corridor between Semberija and Krajina, and this is a land corridor, you have to achieve control not only over the roads in that area but also the surrounding areas. When you look at the map of Bosnia-Herzegovina, say, prior to April 1992, so before the take-overs, you will, of course, see that there are a number of municipalities with a Serbian majority. But there are also municipalities with a non-Serb majority. And since these -- the populations there, the non-Serb populations may well have pursued other goals than the Serbian goal, you have a problem if you want to establish a corridor there, unless you manage to establish Serbian control over those municipalities. And we see, then -- I mean, we see the take-over operations where one of the results is the departure/removal of substantial parts of the non-Serb population in areas where Serbs do not have a majority or only very slim majority. I mean, I can do that for the other goals but I think it's pretty clear -- it's quite clear for the first goal already.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If I can just breakdown the next part of this. How did the strategic goals represent a plan to establish a Serb republic?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, many of the documents -- actually all -- I mean, all the documents that talk about the bigger context: Why are the Bosnian Serbs doing what they are doing or -- or resorting to military means is that they want to stay in Yugoslavia or what remains of Yugoslavia, but the problem is that the other groups in Bosnia-Herzegovina have a different view on that. And, again, I think the ethnic -- the map with the ethnic distribution of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I think have you a 1991 map in the Tribunal, you see how complex the situation is because there is no territorial integrity. So when the Bosnian Serbs political as well as military leadership talk about Serbian lands, the problem is they have a clear view as to how this -- what areas these Serbian lands should cover, but there are a lot of non-Serbs living on these Serbian lands. And in some of the orders, for example, when we refer to Directive number 4 and then subsequent orders --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry, Your Honours. Subsequent orders of the Drina Corps in Eastern Bosnia, it is clearly stated that for what the non-Serbs are concerned, only those that accept Serbian rule will be allowed to stay or are allowed to stay and should even be protected. I've seen documents using the express "loyal Serbs" -- "loyal non-Serbs," I'm sorry, and these people are to stay. The others it is sometimes it's implied but at other times explicitly mentioned that they have to leave. So the -- I think in a nutshell the big problem is: How do you achieve territorial integrity when there are people of different ethnic origin and therefore different concept as to how the future of Bosnia-Herzegovina should look if they are living there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is a good point for me to break. I don't know if it's a good time for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take the break. Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at 25 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While the witness is escorted in the courtroom, I would like to deal with P2505. On the 17th of October of this year, the Chamber asked the Prosecution whether there was an English translation available for the text of one of the maps under P2505. The Prosecution has informally communicated that there is no English translation available, that it does not rely on this text, and that there technical difficulties with redacting the text. And, exceptionally, the Chamber accepts to leave the text unredacted with the clear understanding that the Prosecution does not rely on this text. And that is hereby put on the record. Please be seated, Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, on page 36 of Part 2, you conclude: "The six strategic goals provide the SRBiH TO and subsequently the VRS with a clearly identified set of long-term objectives from which they develop operational and tactical planning documents and conduct military operations throughout the conflict in BiH. The six strategic goals are the basis for Bosnian Serb military operations during the 1992 to 1995 time-period." We'll go through this in more detail throughout the remainder of -- of my examination. But at this time, could you just generally tell us how did Ratko Mladic implement all six of the strategic objectives between 1992 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the most obvious way how the six strategic goals were implemented by General Mladic is through the directives for further operations he signed. Directives for further operations of the VRS, whereby he signed seven out of nine of these directives, and they covered the May 1992 to October/November -- October 1995 time-period.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: On page 117 of Part 2, you conclude that -- and this is something you've mentioned already today, I just want to go further.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: "Even though the take-over operations in northern BiH, as well as other strategically located municipalities in other parts of BiH, are carried out prior to the public announcement of the Bosnian Serb six strategic goals, the pattern in relation to their location, timing, modus operandi, specific objectives, and end state indicate that they represent, in fact, the first phase of the implementation of these six strategic goals." Just so we have a clear reference to this on the record, what time-period are you referring to when you describe this first phrase?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this cover April to May 1992 time-period where we see the take-over by Bosnian Serb forces, including components I have discussed in -- in the report, I mean, also components from outside Bosnia-Herzegovina, of municipalities located in northern Bosnia-Herzegovina. In my conclusion, in order to implement strategic goals number 1 and 2; two being the establishment of a corridor there between semberija, i.e., north-eastern Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the Krajina, i.e., the west.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could you tell us whether this pattern continued once the VRS was formally established in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does, Your Honours, with the difference that whereas during the take-over operations we see different components in these Serb forces. I mentioned them earlier this morning but we see local Serb TO volunteers, volunteers from Serbia, groups affiliated with MUP Serbia. After the establishment of the VRS, the VRS takes -- I mean, the Main Staff takes active steps to subordinate all groups, and then we see the VRS as the main armed forces and in most cases the only armed force conducting operations on the Serbian side in order to implement the goals.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Before going through some of the specific directives, I would like to discuss with you a few documents from May and June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 793.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, this will a 2nd Military District order from General Mladic dated 11 May 1992 standing in -- he is signing -- it's standing -- or it indicates that is he standing in for the commander. This order appears to relate to the carrying out preparations and transfer of JNA units from BiH territory to the FRY. Could you please comment on what you see summarised or what appears before us under items 1 and 2 of this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If we could please scroll down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And could the B/C/S version move to the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you again, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document shows that General Mladic as the -- I mean, actually he is the commander of the 2nd Corps by then. Orders that JNA units that are to withdraw from Bosnia-Herzegovina have to remain -- sorry, have to leave their equipment in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And I mean, this is not explicitly mentioned but he implies only those units that are present in areas under Bosnian Serb control. And then also, I mean, the second paragraph, I mean, it's quite obvious. I think he states that mobilisation should be continued.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If we could go up to the top -- I'm sorry, Mr. Theunens, did you want to add anything else? I didn't people that to cut you off.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, the last sentence of -- I mean, it's just background, but the last sentence of the second paragraph is that - and this is throughout the war - General Mladic insists with the authorities in -- in -- in Serbia and Montenegro, i.e., in FRY, that individuals residing there but who have been born in Bosnia-Herzegovina and who are obviously of Serbian ethnicity should be sent back in order to -- I mean, for those who still have military obligations should return to join the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If we could go -- if we can look at the top of this now. This order is sent to the commands of the 5th, 10th, and 17th, JNA Corps. Could you please tell us which VRS corps were created from these specific corps?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: For what -- the 5th corps is concerned initially its headquarters was in Zagreb, but then obviously during 1991 it had to be moved and ended up in Banja Luka. The 5th Corps forms then -- the 5th JNA Corps, sorry, forms the basis for the 1st Krajina Corps of the VRS. The 17th Corps is a more complex situation because it had its headquarters in Tuzla, so parts of it are withdrawn, and then these parts are transformed in Eastern Bosnia Corps and -- yeah, the Eastern Bosnia Corps. And for the 10th Corps, I need to check my report because I'm not sure any more. Yeah, they used to be in Drvar and they transformed into the 2nd Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have page 2 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: General Mladic, under items 4 and 5 of this order, indicates that corps commanders are personally accountable to him for the implementation of this order and he instructs: "Report to me regularly on the progress of the realisation of this order." Is this consistent with the way in which General Mladic exercised his authority over the corps that he commanded?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. And it's not limited to General Mladic, I would say. I mean, when I was working here before and from documents I reviewed for other cases, this is common knowledge in -- common language, excuse me, in JNA documents, as late as -- as well as VRS later or other armed forces, and it's simply the implementation of the inspection function of command and control.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, could I ask you, is this common in all military organisations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I -- I mean, in -- in the organisation I belonged to, it wouldn't be put as explicitly, but it's implied that you have report about the level of implementation of an order that you have received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that you are accountable for -- to the higher level for whatever is ordered.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it's, I would say, either implied or explicit, it's general military structure.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution tenders 65 ter 793 at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 00793 receives number P3056, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 789. And if we could please slide over just slightly to the left of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No loud speaking, Mr. Mladic, again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This is a 2nd Military District order from Chief of Staff Major-General Manojlo Milovanovic dated 13 May 1992. In the first sentence of this document, we see it states: "Based on the verbal order of lieutenant-general Mladic of 13 May 1992, corps commanders and the commanders of the 580th mabr and 289th, rabr will telephone him every day ..." And then the date of 14 May 1992 is there between 0700 and 0800 hours. First, could you please explain to us how General Mladic is using an oral order in this document; and then if you could subsequently comment for us what does this type of regular reporting, which appears to be twice a day, in the morning and then in the evening, shows.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's nothing unusual about an oral order in -- in a very straightforward matter. That is, that everybody -- I mean, the corps commanders and commanders of -- of units that are directly subordinated to the Main Staff have to report on a regular basis to the commander of the Main Staff so he -- I mean, from the document, it can be concluded General Mladic issued an oral order to, for sure, his Chief of Staff, maybe he did to some corps commanders; but, in any event, the Chief of Staff then transforms this oral order into a written order, which is then forwarded to the subordinate commanders. And the fact that he orders them to report regularly about their activities is not just the inspection function of command and control but also -- I mean, the -- the knowledge that -- or the common principle, I'm sorry, that as a commander he has to be familiar with the situation of his subordinate units two levels down in order to take decisions on the use of his of -- of -- of his units.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In Part 1, you discuss the role of oral orders on page 34 and 43, and you mention oral reports on page 45. Is General Mladic's use of oral orders and reporting in this document consistent with SFRY armed forces doctrine?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do oral orders carry the same weight as written orders?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they do, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: At this time, the Prosecution tenders 65 ter 789 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar -- Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can we have an idea of the provenance of the document? Is it an official document or is it from some unofficial collection?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I see -- if I could please have the evidence registration number up at the top. I'm sorry, this is the one I happen not to have with me. Your Honour, this comes from the VRS Main Staff archives, received by the Office of the Prosecutor on 18 October 2006.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Then we have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It's -- if I could be more detailed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether any further details are -- if you want to change the information, that's different.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If I could add, it's the archives based in the Kozara barracks in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We had already the green light from the Defence. In the assumption that the parties take no issue with a small mistake which is that, in the English, the semi-last word says the 289th; whereas, the original says the 389th as -- further down in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Further down in English, please. There we are. 289th. I take it that you will not take issue with that and that we don't need to upload a new version of it. Madam Registrar, the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 00789 receives number P3057, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have Exhibit P44 -- excuse me, P466.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This is a document from your report. It's an order from the commander of the Birac Brigade to the Zvornik TO dated 28 May 1992. Item 6 of this order states: "The moving out of the Muslim population must be organised and co-ordinated with the municipalities through which the moving out [sic] is carried out. Only women and children can move out, while men fit for military service are placed into camps ..." Do you have any comments on this order?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I mean, the context of the previous discussion, paragraph 6, would be consistent with the first strategic goal, i.e., the separation of the population -- of the -- of the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What level of -- how -- how does this order from a lower command, a brigade level, relate to -- and their actions that are carried out here, relate to the organisation and co-ordination, both with the municipalities and, if any, its superior commands?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand the question. But I would say it is, as -- as we have discussed several times already, it's the implementation of the command and control process and applying -- or abiding with its principles, i.e., single command, unity, and the obligation to implement decisions. So the actions that are ordered by a subordinate commander have to be coherent with the tasks set by the superior commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution now please have 65 ter 00864. Mr. Theunens, this is an another document in your report, in Part 2. It is a 1 June 1992 document from Major Pero Despotovic of the Ilidza Brigade. What does this order show?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I have tried to -- to briefly describe in my report, that is, that in spring 1992, Serbian municipalities are established in -- in areas with a Serb majority. And these lower-level political bodies play a role in mobilisation and so on. Mobilisation of Serbs into, first, local Serb TO, and then, subsequently, also in the VRS. In the time -- in the time of SFRY, we did have secretariats for national defence at lower level, but those were operating in the context of the SFRY armed forces, but the Bosnian Serbs rely on existing structures or they establish their own structures but operating in a similar manner as the other ones. And here, General Mladic issues an order to the Secretariat for National Defence in order to -- to assist with mobilisation of -- of -- of -- yeah, of able-bodied population for the benefit of -- of -- of the VRS, i.e., a brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution at this time tenders this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 00864 receives number P3058, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have Exhibit P353, page 93 of the English, and page 93 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, coming up before you will be an entry from General Mladic's notebooks dated 6 June 1992 regarding consultations on the military and political situation in SRBH. We see that the location for this is indicated as being Jahorina. At the beginning of the notes, it says: Present, leading representatives of the state and political leadership." Did you review this entry during proofing?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes -- yes, I did, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: There are four items on the agenda of this meeting, which continues onto the next page in both versions. The first one is the debate on the borders of SRBiH; the second is the border of Romanija-Birac region; the third one is providing for civilians and refugees; and the fourth is political and military doctrine for upcoming war objectives. If we could have the next page in the B/C/S also, please. On this page, we see that, according to these notes, that Radovan Karadzic opens this meeting and references: "The SRBH Assembly defined the strategic aims." He then comments on a number of other things, including losses during the war, and references to the Croat/Muslim, Croat coalition --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could the English version be enlarged, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: A little bit after this, the notes indicate that Karadzic reiterates the strategic objectives with comments and explanations. What are the strategic objectives that are being referred to at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the six strategic goals as they were presented by Mr. Karadzic at the 16th Assembly Session on the 12th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Does this meeting relate at all to the planning function of command and control?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, it -- it could. I don't know whether any military planning is really discussed at this stage. It seems mainly political. Maybe the next page is going to military issues. But if it goes into military issues, yes, then -- then the military will implement the political tasks, and they are be being planned from what we can read here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If we could continue with this, and then maybe I'll come back to that, to page 97 in both versions. On this page, we see that Karadzic indicates: "The birth of a state and the creation of borders does not occur without war." He then notes the things that are important for demarcating borders. Among those items are: "According to the map, we have 66 per cent of the territory which the world would deny us." What does this comment refer to?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It can mean two things, Your Honours. It can mean that the VRS, at that stage, control 66 per cent of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or - but I think that's a less likely option - that 66 per cent of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina -- that 66 per cent of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina should, according to Mr. Karadzic, belong to the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The next item states: "1.920.000 inhabitants would fit into this map." Do you have any comments on what Karadzic is referring to?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't analysed that. I know at that stage the Bosnian Serbs are approximately, say, yeah, 33 per cent of the population of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but I haven't -- I mean, I haven't seen this -- this notebook prior to arriving here for the proofing, so I have not been able to look into what the meaning of what this figure was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have page 101 of both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: On this page, there's a note -- notation which appears to appear after individual reports from municipalities. Under the one from Bratunac municipality, the entry states: "There are no Muslims now in Bratunac municipality. It is a fully liberated town. There are even no villages which cut off the roads? "Srebrenica municipality is at half. Srebrenica is empty. "90 per cent of the area is bauxite or we have agreed to divide Srebrenica half and half and to have them stay in the area" -- If we need the next page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You left out at small portion [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... before the bauxite --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... if I misread it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... mine. It is an area which is described as -- but it now disappeared in the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: My apologies, Your Honour, I was just trying to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Please proceed. The reference is to a specific area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: "Have them stay in the area of Osmace. "Zvornik will fall with the fall of Bratunac." What does this show about the status of operations in Eastern Bosnia as of June 1992?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In general terms, Your Honours, it shows that the Bosnian Serbs have achieved control over a number of territories there, which would be consistent with the implementation of strategic goal number three, i.e., eliminating the Drina as a border. And the comments of Mr. Karadzic on -- on the -- on the ethnic makeup would be consistent with strategic goal number 1, i.e., the separation of the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have page 108 of both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: At this same 6 June 1992 meeting, General Mladic notes comments from Momcilo Krajisnik. These comments begin: "The goal was to form and unite the Birac-Romanija area." Could you tell us quickly what this strategic goal is.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this -- this -- Your Honours, this refers to northeastern Boris-Herzegovina. I mean, it is partly strategic goal number 2; the corridor. And mainly, of course, eliminating the Drina as a border; strategic number 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: According to the notes, Krajisnik continues: "To draw the borders of this area into include a number of locations," among them Hadzici, Ilidzja, Nova Sarajevo? And then states: "Dobrinja, if we can take it." And then he continues on to list a number of places and ends with the quote: "This should be defended. That will be ours." First of all, could you confirm whether or not these locations being referred to are in and around Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Your Honours. This refers to -- to the western part of Sarajevo in the wider vicinity of the airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: On this page and continuing onto the next, the notes indicate Krajisnik states: "The border has to be defended and held. As of tomorrow" -- I believe it's on the next page of the -- both versions. "As of tomorrow, we have to conquer what is ours and be prepared to defend our state." The date of this meeting is 6 June 1992. On this same date, did General Mladic issue operational directive number 1 concerning forthcoming VRS operations?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a good break time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber -- yes. Mr. Theunens, we'd like to see you back tomorrow, because we will adjourn for the day. We'd like to see you back at 9.30 in the morning. But I first instruct you not to speak or communicate in whatever way, with whomever, about your testimony, either given or still to be given.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, you asked for eight hours. If you would be on track, you would finish tomorrow. Is that ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you would allow me to just review the transcript so far and look at the report overnight, I would be happy to report to Your Honours first thing in the morning on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then if the answer is, No, I'm not going to finish, what would you then expect the Chamber to do?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could even have a couple of hours after -- after court today to -- to let you know as soon as I possibly can in looking at the transcript and what has been admitted so far and what is coming up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you have used four and a half hours by now. So there are three and a half hours left of the eight hours. And I'm not without reason raising this issue with you because there comes a moment where hours are translated into minutes, and minutes are translated into seconds. The Chamber urges you to stick to your time-limit. We adjourn for the day, and we'll resume tomorrow, Friday, the 6th of December, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, II.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I was just informed by Mr. Mladic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One -- one second, Mr. Lukic. Yes. We do not adjourn yet for the day --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Mladic just informed me that he would waive his right to be present tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm looking at Mr. Mladic, and he confirms that you are waiving your right to be absent tomorrow. I see Mr. Mladic is nodding in the affirmative. Therefore, we now then finally adjourn for the day, and we'll resume tomorrow, the 6th, at 9.30 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
